evidence: Invite students to take out their Patterns of the Moon notes sheets. Remind them that they will use these notes and take turns responding to their group members' ideas.
rationale: The standard's four purposes form an OR list; any one student-performed purpose yields full. In this lesson, students make use of multiple texts — the Patterns of the Moon anchor chart, the book Does the Sun Sleep?: Noticing Sun, Moon, and Stars Patterns, and the Sun, Moon, and Stars Word Wall — to build knowledge about why the moon seems to change shape and then to share that information and ideas with classmates during a structured Science Talk. Students actively use these texts when they record personal notes on the Patterns of the Moon notes sheet ("they should record only the information that they think is most important") and then deploy those text-based notes in small-group discussion: "Invite students to take out their Patterns of the Moon notes sheets. Remind them that they will use these notes and take turns responding to their group members' ideas." This satisfies at least the "build knowledge" and "share information and ideas" purposes, with the student as the actor throughout.

evidence: Remind students that they need to record their notes in a way that is useful to them, maybe with pictures and only a few words, so they can read from their notes and use them as evidence in the Science Talk. They should record only the information that they think is most important.
rationale: Both clauses are partially met. For the linking clause, students write individual notes on the Patterns of the Moon notes sheet using information from the anchor chart ("they need to record their notes in a way that is useful to them … They should record only the information that they think is most important"), which is a rudimentary form of linking ideas to a source plan; however, the notes are informal jottings for an oral Science Talk, not a structured linking of ideas to an organizational plan for a composed text. For the highlighting clause, students select the most important information during a turn-and-talk ("What information do you think is most important to know…") and then record only that information, but the prioritization is largely teacher-guided (the teacher stars the anchor chart) and the student product does not formally highlight or emphasize the most relevant points within a constructed text. The standard is tagged (C) — construction — and the lesson's construction artifact (personal notes) is thin relative to the standard's expectation of linking and highlighting within an organizational plan.
standard_raw_text: Link ideas and information to the organization plan, highlighting ideas and information that are most relevant, useful, and impactful. (C)

evidence: Remind students to use the Prepositions anchor chart and Adjectives anchor chart, and the Sun, Moon, and Stars Word Wall as necessary.
rationale: The standard requires students to use descriptive words to craft engaging texts (a Construction act). In the Sky Notebook independent writing (Closing A, p. 293), students are directed to "use the Prepositions anchor chart and Adjectives anchor chart, and the Sun, Moon, and Stars Word Wall" while composing their observations, and teacher feedback confirms at least one student selected the descriptive adjective "glowing." This partially meets the descriptive-words clause because the lesson's primary objective is recording scientific observations, not intentionally crafting with descriptive language — the adjective/preposition use is supportive scaffolding rather than the instructional focus. The "craft engaging texts" clause is not met: no activity in the lesson has students compose a text with the goal of engaging a reader; the writing tasks (notes sheets, Sky Notebook entries, shared writing) are all observational/informational recordings, not texts crafted for audience engagement.

evidence: Remind them that they used this protocol in Lesson 6 and review as necessary using the Science Talk Protocol anchor chart.
rationale: The lesson partially aligns with 1.P.EICC.1.e. Students discuss content in small groups during the Science Talk protocol ("Invite students to take their Patterns of the Moon notes sheet and move into pre-determined groups … Guide students through the protocol"), share their individual writing (Patterns of the Moon notes sheets) with group members, and listen as others share ("How will you show your partner you are listening to him or her?" — students respond: "use eye contact; answer the questions they ask me"). Group norms are reviewed and applied but not newly developed in this lesson, so that clause is only partially met. Students build on peers' ideas using sentence frames ("I'd like to add ___"), which is adjacent to offering feedback but does not constitute evaluative feedback on peers' writing — partially met. There is no moment where students respond to feedback received on their own writing — that clause is not met.
